items.body:
U.S. futures are relatively unchanged after the U.S. Treasury Department said it would at least double the size of its bond buybacks, and oil prices shot higher.

The planned purchases of longer-term government debt by the Treasury could ease pressure on share prices since the maneuver would push bond yields down.

Futures for the S&P 500 were little changed on Thursday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.1 per cent. Nasdaq futures gained 0.1 per cent.

Oil prices rose sharply after ballistic missile fire in United Arab Emirates triggered nationwide warnings residents there, the first time in weeks such an alarm had sounded. President Donald Trump threatened to increase economic pressure on Iran, creating more doubts about a near-term solution to the conflict.

Brent crude, the international standard, surged 2.5 per cent to US$93.90 a barrel. It was trading at roughly US$72 per barrel before the war.

U.S. benchmark crude jumped 2.8 per cent to US$86.72 a barrel.

Yields on U.S. government bonds fell after the Treasury announcement. Yields have risen in recent months over growing concerns about inflation stemming from the conflict in Iran and ballooning government debt.

The national debt surpassed a record US$40 trillion on Wednesday with defense spending soaring and the U.S. involvement in the Middle East.

The yield on the U.S. 10-year Treasury fell to 4.68 per cent on Thursday, although it’s still well above its levels from before the start of the war in Iran. The 30-year Treasury yield fell to around 5.22 per cent.

In Asia, bond yields also eased after the U.S. Treasury’s announcement. Japan’s 10-year government bond yield fell to around 2.85 per cent. It has been trading near 30-year highs.

Walmart’s stock slid more than 6 per cent before the market open on Thursday as the retail giant gave a cautious outlook for the year. Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base.

Investors are also awaiting the latest U.S. unemployment data. The previous report from the Labor Department said that 209,000 people filed jobless claims two weeks ago, up from a revised 200,000 the week before and higher than the 205,000 forecasters had expected.

In Europe, Germany’s DAX fell 0.5 per cent to 25,960.44, while the CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.4 per cent to 8,466.75. Britain’s FTSE 100 shed 0.3 per cent to 10,707.92. Asian shares traded higher.

The U.S. dollar rose to 158.50 Japanese yen from 158.16 yen. The euro was trading at US$1.1696, up from US$1.1677.

Chan Ho-him And Michelle Chapman, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: Trump is talking about the project again five years after it was shut down by Biden when he was president. Here's everything you need to know.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump hinted that he may revive an old pipeline project that would export oil from Canada to the U.S. as part of a pending trade deal.

In a Truth Social post shared Tuesday night, Trump said he had suspended the 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods for three days, two hours before they were set to take place on Wednesday.

The deal, he stated, may include revitalizing the Keystone XL pipeline, a long hotly-contested project that has been in the works for almost a decade.

Trump had attempted to revive the project during his first presidency as part of his then-campaign promises, but the pipeline was quashed by Joe Biden in the first year of his term.

“The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!” Trump’s social media post reads.

He then published an AI-generated image of himself hoisting the Keystone XL pipeline out of a gravesite marked by a tombstone labelled “BURIED BY BIDEN.”

Prime Minister Carney did not mention the pipeline in his own statement on Trump’s announcement.

“Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done,” read the statement.

First proposed in 2008, the project has seen a rocky journey, piled with legal barriers, opposition from environmental and Indigenous activists, and subject to the whims of U.S presidents at different points in time.

What is Keystone XL?

It has been proposed as an expansion project that would carry Canadian crude oil to the U.S. Gulf Coast and, if built, potentially increase those exports to the U.S. by more than 12 per cent.

The current Keystone pipeline, first proposed in 2005 and built between 2008 and 2010, runs from Hardisty, Alta., across Saskatchewan and Manitoba and before crossing the U.S. near Haskett, Man., into North Dakota, Illinois and Nebraska.

Keystone XL, if it had gone ahead, would have seen a direct route built between Hardisty and Steele City, Neb.

However, only the U.S. portions of the extension have been constructed so far.

How was it initially approved?

The project was first proposed in 2008 by its then-owners TC Energy Corp. and ConocoPhilips. At the time, TC Energy Corp. was called TransCanada Corp.

The Canadian Energy Board approved the project in 2010, but that came with 22 conditions on safety, environmental protection and landowner rights.

Then-U.S. president Barack Obama was the first to shut it down two years later, in January 2012.

Why is it so controversial?

The project has seen major opposition from legislators and activists, citing environmental concerns, lack of legal oversight and unconstitutional use of state law to review the routes.

Obama rejected the project in 2012 after U.S. legislators passed a bill in December 2011 that stated the president had to make a decision on the pipeline’s future in 60 days.

Obama argued that this did not allow much time to review the new route but said TransCanada was free to submit another application.

Between 2012 and 2016, project costs ballooned as TransCanada looked to build southern legs of the expansion. While the company found favour in the Nebraska state government and a Republican-led U.S. Congress, the project was repeatedly shot down through legal challenges from pipeline opponents and a veto from the Obama administration.

Trump, in his 2016 presidential campaign, vowed to bring back the project if elected. In January 2017, he signed an executive order approving the project with plans to renegotiate the terms.

The project still faced legal challenges over the next two years with construction getting underway in April 2020. In November, Biden was elected president and shut down the project on his first day of presidency.

Why did Biden cancel the project?

Biden cancelled the project in January 2021, stating that it did not align with his administration’s economic and environmental objectives.

He had served as U.S. vice-president during the Obama administration.

Then-Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau expressed disappointment over the cancellation and stated that his representatives were pressing the Biden administration to reconsider.

Then-Alberta premier Jason Kenney threatened legal action if the project was scrapped.

What has happened since?

The project remained buried until Trump entered his second term as president.

In February 2025, Trump posted on social media that he wanted to revive the Keystone XL project.

In October, Carney pitched the project to Trump in exchange for relief from U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs on Canada’s industries, to which Trump was “very receptive,” according to media reports published then.

In March, Alberta Liberal MP Corey Hogan confirmed that the pipeline was being used as leverage in trade talks with the U.S.

“As we start thinking about some of the exposed industries and some of those that are really being hit hard by tariffs, we’ve got to have things to negotiate with, and energy is one of those things,” Hogan told CTV’s Power Play at the time.

He added it would be “foolish” for the federal government not to “think about the opportunities” the pipeline project could provide.

While the pipeline did not appear to be part of the pending trade deal, it could become a “sticking point” for Trump, according to CTV News political analyst Eric Ham.

He told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that the situation seems “mysterious,” but noted Trump has prioritized “oil and energy” as a key component in his administration and in negotiations with Canada and other countries.

“We saw how the president was willing to invade, frankly, Venezuela over energy,” Ham said. “So this has always been a priority.”

Who will benefit from the pipeline?

“It’s really one of those unique cases where I think both countries benefit,” said Dennis McConaghy, a former Canadian energy executive, on Thursday.

In an interview with CTV Your Morning, McConaghy explained that Canada would benefit economically since Canadian heavy oil suits U.S. refineries.

“Now the argument has always been Canada might gain more economic margin by sending its incremental oil production to the West Coast,” McConaghy said. “Of course, that means you have to be able to get a pipeline built to the West Coast, and that’s always had obvious risks.”

items.body:
Cryptocurrency and blockchain-related stocks surged in premarket trading on Thursday after U.S. President Donald Trump urged Congress to pass legislation establishing clear rules for the digital asset sector, following a White House meeting with industry executives.

Trump, a vocal cryptocurrency advocate who has promised to make the U.S. the “crypto capital of the world,” called on lawmakers to pass a “fair version of the Clarity Act,” an industry-backed bill stalled in the Senate.

The act, if enacted, would define whether cryptocurrency qualifies as a security or a commodity, clarifying jurisdiction between the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission over the sector.

Industry executives and analysts say that without legislation, regulations are vulnerable to shifting political winds and court challenges.

  • Latest updates on crypto news here

However, many Democrats, and some Republicans, say they would not support a bill without strong language banning political officials, including Trump, from profiting from their own crypto ventures.

President Trump disclosed more than US$1.4 billion in earnings from his family’s crypto ventures in 2025.

Bitcoin BTC=, the world’s largest cryptocurrency, rose 3.4 per cent and pushed through resistance levels that had held since early June, moving past the US$70,000 mark to highs of about US$71,700. Ether ETH= gained 3.3 per cent, its highest level in over three months.

The moves mirror the boost the sector received when the GENIUS Act was signed into law in July 2025, establishing a regulatory framework for stablecoins.

Crypto exchange Coinbase Global gained 8.4 per cent, while bitcoin bull Strategy rose 10 per cent. Miners Riot Platforms RIOT.O, MARA Holdings MARA.O, Hut 8 HUT.O and Bit Digital BTBT.O rose between 3 per cent and 6 per cent.

Bitcoin mining machine maker Canaan CAN.O surged 20 per cent, stablecoin issuer Circle CRCL.N gained 8 per cent and retail trading platform Robinhood Markets HOOD.O advanced 5 per cent.

The gains come despite a broader 2026 slump. Bitcoin has lost about 18 per cent so far this year.

(Reporting by Pritam Biswas and Arasu Kannagi Basil in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid)

items._ogDesc: China’s Alibaba reported a 9 per cent rise in quarterly revenue on Thursday, as strong AI demand fueled growth in its cloud business, but missed estimates for adjusted profit due to heavy capital expenditure.
items.body:
China’s Alibaba reported a 9 per cent rise in quarterly revenue on Thursday, as strong AI demand fueled growth in its cloud business, but missed estimates for adjusted profit due to heavy capital expenditure.

As businesses deploy AI, demand for the cloud computing power needed to train and run those systems has surged, benefiting China’s largest technology companies.

Alibaba, the country’s biggest cloud services provider, has stepped up investment in AI infrastructure, proprietary models and applications, positioning the technology as a key growth driver for its cloud and consumer businesses.

The company’s AI cloud and compute services revenue rose 45 per cent to 48.44 billion yuan (US$7.21 billion) in the quarter.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Alibaba’s adjusted earnings per American Depositary Share of 8.52 yuan missed estimates of 10.53 yuan and its U.S.-listed shares fell 2.6 per cent in premarket trading.

“We delivered a strong quarter, driven by the improving commercialization of our full stack AI capabilities,” Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu said in a statement.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Alibaba’s capital expenditure rose 75 per cent to 67.68 billion yuan in the quarter ended June 30, as it continued to invest in AI infrastructure.

The company reported revenue of 268.95 billion yuan in the first quarter, compared with an average analyst estimate of 268.88 billion yuan, data compiled by LSEG showed. Its net income for the quarter tumbled 75 per cent.

CHINESE AI RACE

Alibaba is locked in a battle with other Chinese tech giants and startups to release more capable open-weight frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost of proprietary U.S. offerings like Anthropic’s Claude, highlighting the rapid pace of advancement of Chinese AI models and their shorter release cycles.

But as competition heats up, firms are pivoting towards offering better agentic and coding capabilities to capture more of China’s lucrative domestic enterprise market.

“As synergies across our core businesses deepen and AI monetization ramps up, we have greater strategic and financial flexibility to make disciplined and sustained investments in full-stack AI capabilities,” Toby Xu, Alibaba’s chief financial officer, said in a statement.

Alibaba is also a major investor in other Chinese frontier AI startups including Moonshot, and supplies it with cloud computing infrastructure.

Earlier this year Alibaba split ​its AI businesses from its cloud computing arm and tasked Wu with leading the “Alibaba Token Hub” ​group, as it races ⁠to make its AI segment profitable.

Alibaba’s fintech affiliate Ant Group reported 1 per cent year-on-year growth in quarterly profit, Reuters calculations showed, as it has attempted to pivot towards agentic AI commerce, AI digital health applications and embodied AI models in recent years.

(Reporting by Harshita Mary Varghese in Bengaluru and Laurie Chen in Beijing; Editing by Maju Samuel and Alexander Smith )

items._ogDesc: Deere , the world’s largest farm equipment manufacturer, raised its full-year net income forecast on Thursday and posted its first rise in quarterly profit in three years on the back of an AI-driven construction boom and tariff refunds.
items.body:
Deere , the world’s largest farm equipment manufacturer, raised its full-year net income forecast on Thursday and posted its first rise in quarterly profit in three years on the back of an AI-driven construction boom and tariff refunds.

Rising U.S. government and private spending on infrastructure alongside the vast AI-fueled buildout of data centers has lifted demand for construction equipment, with Deere’s construction and forestry segment emerging as its fastest-growing business. Net sales in the segment rose 18 per cent from a year earlier.

The trend has helped the company weather a prolonged lull in demand for its large tractors and combine harvesters amid rising costs and falling agricultural yields.

Deere’s Small Ag & Turf segment — home to low horsepower tractors often used in dairy farming — posted a 12 per cent rise in net sales, with demand aided by improving prices for milk and beef.

Revenue at its mainstay Production & Precision Agriculture segment, which includes its large green tractors and combine harvesters, dropped 6 per cent from a year earlier. CEO John C. May, however, said Deere continues “to believe 2026 will mark the bottom of the current ag equipment cycle.”

The company reported a profit of US$5.10 per share for the quarter ended August 2, up from US$4.75 per share a year earlier and above analysts’ estimates of US$4.70 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG.

Its quarterly revenue rose 6 per cent to US$11 billion, also beating expectations of US$10.73 billion.

Deere’s quarterly profit rise was aided by a tariff refund of US$110 million during the quarter.

The John Deere tractor manufacturer now expects 2026 net income of US$4.75 billion to US$5 billion, compared with its earlier projection of US$4.5 billion to US$5 billion. The midpoint of the new range is in line with Wall Street expectations.

Shares of the company were up 1 per cent in premarket trading, after jumping about 6 per cent earlier in the day.

(Reporting by Nandan Mandayam in Bengaluru; Editing by Jonathan Ananda)

items.title: Chinese court sentences founder of troubled property developer Evergrande to life in prison
items.description: Chinese property developer Hui Ka Yan, founder of the Evergrande real estate group, has been sentenced to life in prison and the companies were fined a total of more than US$2 billion, a court in the southern city of Shenzhen said Thursday.

items._ogDesc: Chinese property developer Hui Ka Yan, founder of the Evergrande real estate group, has been sentenced to life in prison and the companies were fined a total of more than US$2 billion, a court in the southern city of Shenzhen said Thursday.
items.body:
HONG KONG — Chinese property developer Hui Ka Yan, founder of the Evergrande real estate group, has been sentenced to life in prison and the companies were fined a total of more than US$2 billion, a court in the southern city of Shenzhen said Thursday.

The decision marks a milestone in Evergrande’s saga after it collapsed with more than US$300 billion in liabilities when Chinese authorities cracked down on excessive borrowing in the real estate industry in 2020. That triggered a crunch among many developers and brought on a downturn in the property market that has weighed on the broader economy ever since.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People’s Court convicted Hui, 67, and Evergrande of engaging in large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group’s assets and concealing its liabilities.

In a statement, the court also said Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin, abused his position in orchestrating fraud and misappropriating company assets.

Evergrande group was fined 8.82 billion yuan (US$1.31 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group was fined 7 billion yuan (US$1.04 billion), the court said in the statement.

“The amount involved is exceptionally large, the circumstances are particularly egregious, and extraordinarily heavy economic losses have been caused,” the court’s statement said. “The harm to society is extremely serious. Therefore, severe punishment should be given in accordance with the law.”

Hui’s sons, Xu Tenghe and Xu Zhijian, were also sentenced alongside senior Evergrande executives and others linked to the group on charges including illegally taking public deposits, fundraising fraud and the illegal use of funds, China’s official Xinhua News Agency said. A total of more than 50 individuals were sentenced to imprisonment of between 22 months and 18 years, Xinhua said, although a breakdown of sentencing details was not provided.

A photo of Hui’s courtroom appearance released by the Shenzhen court on Thursday showed an aged Hui, who used to be a high-profile figure but had long been out of public view, wearing a navy blue shirt standing in between two uniformed officers behind a sign that read “defendant.”

Hui pleaded guilty in April to various charges including illegal absorption of public deposits, fraud and bribery after he was detained in China.

China Evergrande, founded in 1996, defaulted on its debts in 2021. It was the world’s most heavily indebted real estate developer before it was ordered to liquidate its assets. After Evergrande’s downfall triggered the broader downturn in China’s massive property sector, home prices have fallen by roughly 20 per cent or more since 2021.

Authorities in Hong Kong and mainland China earlier said their investigations found Evergrande had manipulated its financial data by tactics that included prematurely booking revenue from property sales before completion and delivery of the apartments to buyers. Revenues were overstated by roughly US$80 billion over 2019 and 2020, they said.

Hui was fined 47 million yuan (US$6.5 million) in 2024 and banned from China’s securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission over inflating company financial results, among other issues.

Once reported to be China’s richest man, Hui used to own the football club Guangzhou Evergrande. At one point, he and his companies were involved in investing in and building theme parks and electric vehicles.

His story was one of rags-to-riches. Born in 1958 into a rural family in central China’s Henan province, he worked in the steel industry in the 1980s before establishing Evergrande, which then prospered during China’s housing market boom. He was one of many businessmen who have also gained political influence by joining a major advisory organization, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Congress.

Associated Press writer Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

items.body:
OTTAWA — Some premiers say they’re optimistic about Canada’s progress in reaching a trade deal to avoid punishing tariffs from the United States, while others say they’re waiting for more details about the agreement.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced Tuesday he would put a three-day pause on 50 per cent tariffs that would have hit an array of Canadian goods just after midnight Wednesday.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston told reporters Wednesday that he was “optimistic” about the deal, adding that Prime Minister Mark Carney has asked provinces to restock American alcohol on their shelves.

B.C.’s David Eby said that while no agreement will offer everything the country is hoping for, the federal government has made substantial progress across strategic sectors.

Scott Moe of Saskatchewan said Wednesday that he hopes both countries can negotiate a deal that would reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette told reporters it was too soon to make a judgment call about the deal, adding that she needed more information to see whether it’s positive for her province.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 20, 2026.

The Canadian Press staff

items.title: PM Carney asks premiers to remove U.S. booze ban as officials try to finalize trade deal
items.description: Despite cautious optimism around a tentative agreement, provincial sources told CTV News after a briefing with Prime Minister Mark Carney and the premiers that a deal is not done yet.

items._ogDesc: Despite cautious optimism around a tentative agreement, provincial sources told CTV News after a briefing with Prime Minister Mark Carney and the premiers that a deal is not done yet.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said the United States “probably have a deal with Canada” on Wednesday, one day after he delayed new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods, and that the Keystone XL pipeline “may be awoken from the grave.”

Later in the day, Prime Minister Mark Carney met with the nation’s first ministers to discuss the details of a tentative deal, with several premiers confirming that Carney asked provinces and territories to put U.S. booze back on the shelves.

However, multiple provincial sources told CTV News that while they share cautious optimism over a potential agreement, a deal is not done yet.

Here’s everything that happened on Aug. 19, 2026:

PM Carney asks premiers to return U.S. booze to shelves: Houston

Following a virtual first ministers meeting, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said Prime Minister Mark Carney asked the provincial leaders “to return the U.S. alcohol to the shelf.”

In a virtual media conference on Wednesday, Houston said the ask is “something that came directly out of the negotiating table,” and is “something that (he) would be willing to do for the prime minister at this point in time.”

“Whether Nova Scotians or whether Canadians will actually buy it when it gets back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion,” he added.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Provincial sources say trade deal not done yet

Multiple provincial sources are sharing cautious optimism with CTV News following a briefing with Carney on the tentative trade deal between Canada and the U.S. However, they also emphasized that the deal is not done yet.

In a post to Truth Social late Tuesday, Trump said the countries “have a deal,” but sources say that characterization is not accurate and further negotiations are ongoing.

The provincial sources also tell CTV News that Carney personally asked the premiers to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves. He even told them he will bear any public pushback if that happens.

According to a recent Nanos Research survey, most Canadians say they won’t purchase U.S. booze if its returns to stores.

As for the tariff reduction coming to Canada, the sources say half of the impact will be felt in Ontario, with the other half affecting the rest of Canada.

One source indicated that this is enough to get Ontario Premier Doug Ford on board.

Stephanie Ha, bureau manager, Ottawa News Bureau

With files from CTV News’ chief political correspondent Vassy Kapelos

More details on potential deal needed: Quebec premier

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette says she doesn’t have enough information to determine whether the tentative Canada-U.S. tariff deal is a good agreement for her province.

Fréchette spoke to reporters outside her office following a meeting with Carney and the nation’s premiers on a potential agreement before new tariffs were set to take effect Wednesday.

“I have to get more information from Ottawa. I’ve asked many questions, and they have taken note, and we will talk again tomorrow, or maybe Friday. We’ll see,” she said.

“When I get all the information, I’ll be able to decide if it’s a good agreement or not for Quebec,” she added. “I’m here to protect businesses, workers and supply management needs to be maintained; the cultural exception needs to be maintained, and therefore, until I get new information I won’t be able to position myself.”

Robin Della Corte, CTV News Montreal journalist

Read the full story here

Potential deal good for Saskatchewan: Premier Moe

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe told reporters Wednesday that the tentative trade deal between Canada and the U.S. is good for both countries, as well as the province.

“We need to have, in many ways, preferred market access to our largest trading partner,” Moe said. “I feel that is what we’re in the process of achieving.”

While these tariffs have only affected roughly five per cent of the Saskatchewan economy, Moe said the status quo was not possible and negotiators had to find the best path forward with the country’s largest trading partner.

He said the deal means Canada will have the best trade agreement of any country in the world with the United States.

CTV News Saskatoon staff

Read the full story here

U.S. booze could return if deal reached: N.W.T. premier

Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson says the territory is prepared to put U.S. alcohol back on the shelves once Canada and the United States finalize a new trade deal.

He added that Canadians would welcome a return to the close relationship the two countries once had, but recognizes the current circumstances are different.

“I think that we need to accept the reality that those days are gone, and it’s a different trading environment now going forward, with President Trump in the White House,” he said.

Simpson said he isn’t convinced a change in the White House or a different political party would necessarily restore the previous relationship.

“What we need to do is make sure that we can get the best deal that we can get,” he said.

Tammy Ibrahimpoor, CTVNews.ca journalist

Meeting between cabinet, first ministers ‘constructive’: LeBlanc

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the meeting between cabinet and the nation’s premiers was a “constructive and, frankly, very important conversation.”

“The prime minister updated the premiers on where we were in terms of our discussions with the United States,” LeBlanc told reporters Wednesday.

“We have more work to do,” he added before leaving the scrum.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Sectoral tariffs reduced: sources

Multiple sources tell CTV News there are reductions in sectoral tariffs, such as steel and aluminum, as part of the agreement with the United States, but none of the sources knew the scope of those reductions.

As for how the public will respond, sources also tell CTV News the details of those sectorial tariffs will “make or break the deal” politically for Prime Minister Mark Carney.

CTV News Ottawa Bureau

‘Probably have a deal with Canada’: Trump

Speaking to reporters in Washington on Wednesday Trump said the U.S. “probably” has “a deal with Canada.”

“We delayed it for three days, because I think we have a deal with the prime minister and a good deal for everybody,” he said.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

U.S. pays ‘brunt’ of aluminum tariffs: executive

Canada’s aluminum sector is under “major” tariff pressure, but the United States is “paying the brunt of those,” said Aluminium Association of Canada’s president and CEO Jean Simard.

“Right now, the U.S. is paying much more per ton of aluminum than Europe, because basically, they need the metal,” Simard said in an interview with CTV News Channel on Wednesday.

By the fall of 2025, exports of unwrought aluminum and aluminum alloys were down 26 per cent from levels reported the previous November, according to Statistics Canada.

Simard says once the Middle East conflict between the U.S. and Iran began, the American inventory shrank from six weeks to one, meaning Canada could raise the price of aluminum for a U.S. market desperate for product.

“That tension between supply and demand just kept the price going higher,” he said.

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Finish the damn thing’: Former Alberta premier on Keystone pipeline

A former Alberta premier says he’s encouraged by renewed discussions about the Keystone XL Pipeline.

Jason Kenney told CTV News Wednesday it’s time to “just get ‘er done” and expand the project.

“The U.S. does need a reliable secure source of energy, and (this) could be that,” he said. “With this project, we would be.”

The long-abandoned pipeline project starts in Hardisty, Alta., a town northeast of Red Deer.

It would carry Canadian crude to the Gulf Coast.

The expansion was originally proposed in 2008 but was shot down twice by Democrat administrations.

Experts estimate the expansion could increase Canadian crude exports to the U.S. by more than 12 per cent.

“One of the best ways to deal with Trump’s aggression against the Canadian economy is to give him a win, which is also a win for Canada,” Kenney said.

“That would be a big pipeline going south.”

Timm Bruch, CTV News Calgary journalist

Read the full story here

Premier Smith talks pipelines

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith chimed in on Canada’s tentative deal with Trump, which appears to involve the Keystone XL pipeline.

“Alberta wants to build new pipelines west, east, north and south and we are always in discussions with industry to support these opportunities,” she said in a statement on Wednesday.

Smith also urged the federal government to restore free and fair trade with the U.S. “while also diversifying and strengthening the Canadian economy.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Carney to convene cabinet, premiers

Carney will chair a cabinet meeting in Ottawa at 3 p.m. ET, followed by a meeting with premiers at 4:30 p.m. News media have been excluded from both.

CTV News heard earlier from Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office that he will meet Carney in Ottawa.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

LeBlanc breezes past press

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is back on Parliament Hill following a trip home from Washington. He was met by a group of reporters but did not speak to them, beyond saying hello and remarking it’s “less humid” in Ottawa.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Details of potential deal key to ending booze ban: O’Toole

Ahead of a highly anticipated meeting between the prime minister and premiers, former federal Conservative leader Erin O’Toole says the details of a potential deal with the United States will be key in determining whether provinces are prepared to lift bans on American booze.

“The alcohol on shelves is not a Canadian tariff. That’s a decision by the provinces,” O’Toole, who also serves on the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, told CTV News Channel on Wednesday.

“It’s going to come down to the premiers working with the prime minister to say, ‘yeah, we think this deal is good enough for certain sectors and some of our workers, that we will stop this symbolic act of boycotting the U.S. alcohol.’”

Multiple sources tell CTV News there are reductions in sectoral tariffs on the table as part of the agreement with the U.S., including steel and aluminum. However, O’Toole notes it doesn’t seem like there is much talk about any movement on softwood lumber.

“So, I hope that provinces like B.C. and Ontario, will be able to work with the federal government on a made-in-Canada solution.”

Samantha Pope, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos senior producer

Trump says ‘no tariffs going into Canada’

“We have no tariffs going into Canada anymore,” Trump said on Wednesday. “Canada was charging us tremendous tariffs.”

Asked if the U.S. plans to drop any of the tariffs it charges on Canadian autos, Trump said “we’re reducing it a little bit.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump: New deal is ‘great’ for U.S. farmers

Trump says the new agreement with Canada is “great for our farmers” and a “very good deal for both parties.”

He made the remark to reporters in Washington.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

U.S. Ambassador says he welcomes ‘significant progress’

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says he is welcoming the “significant progress” made between Canada and the United States towards a new trade agreement.

Hoekstra released a statement on Wednesday afternoon crediting U.S. President Donald Trump for his “leadership and determination” for driving the negotiations.

He also said he appreciates “the efforts of our Canadian partners in making this possible.”

Hoekstra’s latest comments strike a more conciliatory tone towards Canada than previous months, in which he publicly criticized the provincial ban on U.S. alcohol and welcomed the possibility of Canada becoming the 51st state.

There is currently a Canadian petition calling for his expulsion that has garnered nearly 240,000 signatures.

Stephanie Ha, Bureau Manager, Ottawa News Bureau

LeBlanc: Supply management intact

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says he’s confident that supply management will remain intact.

Canada has implemented a wide range of economic mechanisms to protect its domestic agricultural industry. Those tools include import and production quotas and set pricing. The Americans have raised what it calls “irritants” within that system, and Quebec Premier Christine Frechette called it a “red line” not to be crossed earlier today.

“The prime minister was very clear. We needed to protect supply management. We needed to ensure that the supply management regime remained entirely intact and I’m confident that that’s the case,” LeBlanc said, before abruptly leaving a scrum in Washington.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Keystone XL is ‘encouraging’: Former premier

Jean Charest, a former Quebec premier and current member of the prime minister’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, says it’s “encouraging” that Trump is hinting at the revival of the defunct cross-border Keystone XL pipeline project.

“Whether it’s Keystone or something else on energy, if we’re able to enlarge the conversation beyond tariffs, we’re in a much better position to defend our interests,” Charest told CTV News Channel on Wednesday.

He adds that this also “says a lot” about how Canada-U.S. relations have evolved.

“Canada, from the beginning has argued that our relationship with the United States is about defence. It’s about the border. It’s about immigration. It’s about the Arctic (and) strategic minerals,” Charest said.

“If that’s the case, we’re going to have a much better conversation in which we’re able to defend our interests. So the simple fact that the president raises Keystone XL as being a new possibility is interesting.”

Samantha Pope, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos senior producer

‘Did not see this coming’: Ham on Keystone XL

When it comes to reviving the Keystone XL pipeline, Trump has brought up an issue that many people “did not see coming,” according to CTV News political analyst Eric Ham.

Ham called it a “clearly polarizing issue,” noting that it was rejected under the Obama administration and brought back during Trump’s earlier term in 2016, before being rejected again by former U.S. president Joe Biden.

Now Trump says it is now back on the table.

“I think the question, given that we know how intractable these issues are: Can they actually get this negotiation done in 72 hours?” Ham asked.

According to the political analyst, it seems “quite insurmountable” that this can be ironed out within three days.

Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca journalist

No more concessions: NDP’s Lewis to PM Carney

NDP Leader Avi Lewis is urging Prime Minister Mark Carney not to grant “any concessions that would further undermine our economic independence” during trade negotiations with the U.S.

“We are dealing with a president who trades in chaos and unpredictability: there is no deal that will bring an end to the threats and uncertainty,” Lewis said in a social media post Wednesday.

For this reason, the NDP leader said it’s essential to protect Canadian workers “without granting further unilateral concessions.”

He added that the Keystone XL pipeline that Trump said the tentative deal could revive is “a concession that makes no sense whatsoever - for our economy, our sovereignty, or the climate.”

“No deal is better than a bad deal,” Lewis wrote to Carney.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Keystone XL pipeline is ‘encouraging’: Former Quebec premier

Jean Charest, a former Quebec premier and current member of the prime minister’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, says it’s “encouraging” that Trump is hinting at the revival of the defunct cross-border Keystone XL pipeline project.

“Whether it’s Keystone or something else on energy, if we’re able to enlarge the conversation beyond tariffs, we’re in a much better position to defend our interests,” Charest told CTV News Channel on Wednesday.

He adds that this also “says a lot” about how Canada-U.S. relations have evolved.

“Canada, from the beginning has argued that our relationship with the United States is about defence. It’s about the border. It’s about immigration. It’s about the Arctic (and) strategic minerals,” Charest says.

“If that’s the case, we’re going to have a much better conversation in which we’re able to defend our interests. So the simple fact that the president raises Keystone XL as being a new possibility is interesting.”

Samantha Pope, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos senior producer

The ‘Canadian advantage’

Carney congratulated Canadian and U.S. negotiators for “significant progress” on trade.

The agreement, which has not been released, “reinforces” the “Canadian advantage,” Carney wrote on X.

LeBlanc coming home

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is heading back from Washington to Ottawa.

“Minister LeBlanc is heading back to Ottawa to meet with the prime minister and take other meetings necessary to finalise trade negotiations,” reads a statement from the minister’s office.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Keystone XL could be ‘sticking point’ for Trump

Bringing back the cross-border oil pipeline did not appear to be part of the pending trade deal, but it could become a “sticking point,” according to CTV News political analyst Eric Ham.

He told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that the situation seems “mysterious,” but noted Trump has prioritized “oil and energy” as a key component in his administration and in negotiations with Canada and other countries.

“We saw how the president was willing to invade, frankly, Venezuela over energy,” Ham said. “So this has always been a priority.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Keystone XL is already ‘revived’

The Keystone XL project has already been revived, a Canadian policy analyst said, despite Trump stating intentions to revive it in a trade announcement this week.

The proposal had always been “approved on the Canadian side,” Heather Exner-Piros, director of energy, natural resources, and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, an Ottawa think tank.

She added that South Bow, which now owns the project, has already entered into an agreement with American company Bridger to revive it.

Producers have already contracted out a portion of the pipeline and are planning a final investment decision in 2027.

“No one is disappointed that Donald Trump is latching himself on to this, but it wasn’t really a part of the negotiations,” she said.

The project already had commercial backing and private financing, she added, with the intention of “expanding production generally.”

Trump “has this idea of energy dominance,” she said.

“Having those Canadian sources of oil coming in, bolstering supply ... is important for the United States. And if Donald Trump wants to take credit for it, I say go ahead.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Probably no good options’: Toronto board of trade head

The president and CEO of the Toronto Region Board of Trade says that while he’s “cautiously optimistic” about Canada potentially reaching a deal with the U.S., he understands significant concessions were likely made as a result.

“There are probably no good options in this negotiation,” Giles Gherson told CP24 Wednesday afternoon.

As consumers and businesses on both sides of the border anxiously await the details of a possible agreement, Gherson said seeing auto tariffs dropped would be a strong start.

“We would like to see them eliminated. We’ve had free trade in automotive since 1965 between Canada and the United States, and then all of a sudden we’ve been hit with these with these significant tariffs, which have really done significant damage to our sector.”

Gherson went on to explain that any deal reached by Canada and the U.S. would essentially act as a “ceasefire” in Trump’s trade war, but pointed out that any pause in the trade dispute would be temporary until CUSMA renegotiations open next year.

“And the question is: how much do we have to pay for the ceasefire?”

Phil Tsekouras, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Merged into one piece’

Former Conservative deputy leader Lisa Raitt says the brief reporter scrum with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has raised some questions: Was LeBlanc nodding while Greer spoke because he understood what his counterpart was saying, or because he was in agreement?

“It’s interesting that one side, the U.S. is saying that it is a win, and the Canadian side is saying it’s an extension to negotiate for three more days,” she told CTV News Channel. “Is this an extension so that the minister and the prime minister can speak to the premiers and speak to the industry sector heads that are going to be impacted by whatever deal has been struck at the table?”

Raitt, who is also a member of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, adds that the council has been told there will be an opportunity to address other issues with the U.S., like digital strategy, oil provisions and critical minerals, once trade has been stabilized and the tariffs are negotiated away.

“I thought those things were going to be the second step, and it looks like everything has been merged into one piece,” she says. “We’ll have to see where we ended up in the whole spectrum.”

Samantha Pope, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos senior producer

Greer: A North American ‘powerhouse’

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, speaking to reporters following a brief meeting with Canadian negotiators, said his team is “very happy with where we ended up.”

He said the agreement, the details for which have not been released, will “really strengthen the North American economy” as an energy and manufacturing “powerhouse.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

American distillers ‘hopeful’ for return to Canadian shelves

The U.S. spirits industry is keeping a close eye on this potential trade deal and hoping for a quick return to Canadian liquor stores.

“The United States exports about US$220-million worth of American spirits to Canada, and that’s all but been shattered,” Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, told CTV News Channel.

All but two Canadian provinces and territories have banned the sale of U.S. alcoholic products from government liquor stores in retaliation to U.S. trade action against Canada. U.S. products remain available in Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Swonger says he’s hopeful provincial premiers will support the prime minister in getting a deal done and returning American alcohol to the shelves.

“Let the brands work hard to try to earn Canadian consumers back,” Swonger said.

Tiffany Hendsbee, CTVNews.ca Supervising Multiplatform Writer

Canadian reps remain quiet: Conservative analyst

Canadian trade representatives are sharing little information on the trade negotiations, a Conservative analyst says.

Kate Harrison told CTV News Channel on Wednesday that Canadians are receiving more updates from the U.S. on the pending deal and what’s being discussed.

This belies previous campaign promises made by Carney to secure a trade deal that was better than the one before, she said.

“It doesn’t instill much confidence,” she added.

“We have a stay of execution for 72 hours. I think a lot of Canadians are going to be asking, ‘What have we given up to get even that momentary reprieve?’”

Canada, for example, has not stated whether Keystone XL, a cross-border oil pipeline will be revived as part of the deal, nor have there been comments on whether alcohol is back on the table.

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Conservatives’ plan for U.S. trade deal

Canada can offer U.S. a national strategic mineral and oil reserve as a lever in the pending trade deal, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Wednesday.

Poilievre told reporters in Charlottetown, P.E.I. that Canada can offer a “tailor-made reserve” of strategic resources to offer to countries with tariff-free trade.

Canada has 10 of the 12 NATO-defined strategic minerals needed to fight a war, he said and is the fourth-biggest supplier of oil.

“The Americans need all of those things,” he said.

He also outlined a “tariff-free auto pact” wherein for every car manufactured in Canada, the same producer can get a car to sell duty free from a partner in CUSMA.

He advocated for six-month approval times for major projects, with one project undergoing one review.

“We should bundle all of this up in a Canadian Sovereignty Act, and we should use the aforementioned leverage to get the deal that we want,“ he said.

”We always have to put our country first, and Conservatives are fighting for Canada.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Poilievre says he hasn’t heard from Carney

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says he has not heard from the prime minister on trade negotiations since the tariff threats were first announced.

“Mr. Carney has refused to have any help from anybody,” Poilievre told reporters on Wednesday in Charlottetown, P.E.I.

However, Poilievre said he is willing to put differences aside to obtain a deal that will end tariffs in Canada.

“I’ve (offered) numerous times in our phone calls,” he said. “When I went to the (U.S.), I very clearly refused to criticize him on foreign soil. I briefed him on my visit and my meetings ... and our MPs have reached out again and again to the government to offer any help we can.”

He reiterated wanting to see a deal that is, as “promised” by Carney, better than the previous one.

“Before we had basically no tariffs on goods coming to the United States,” he said. “...We still want to make sure that he keeps his word and gets the great deal, the even better deal that he promised Canadians.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Read Trump’s statement

Trump posted the following message on his Truth Social platform late Tuesday evening.

“I have paused the 50% Tariffs against Canada, that were scheduled to kick in tomorrow morning for a three day period, based on the fact that Canada and the U.S.A., subject to the finalization of documents, have a DEAL! The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

He then published an AI-generated image of himself hoisting the Keystone XL out of a gravesite marked by a tombstone labelled “BURIED BY BIDEN.”

Read Carney’s statement

Carney posted this message online on Tuesday.

“Over the last number of weeks, Canada has engaged in intensive discussions with the United States to address outstanding trade issues and deliver greater certainty and real benefits for Canadian businesses, workers, farmers, and families.

“Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done. As this work is ongoing, the United States has agreed to postpone the implementation of its 50% tariff on a range of Canadian goods under Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act of 1930 until end of day, August 21.

items._ogDesc: The British Columbia government has issued a new temporary protection order for the Salmon River watershed, where chinook salmon have returned to spawn.
items.body:
The British Columbia government has issued a new temporary protection order for the Salmon River watershed, where chinook salmon have returned to spawn.

The Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship says in a news release that the order aims to ensure enough water remains in the river amid ongoing drought conditions and low streamflow, which threaten fish survival.

It says technical staff have been monitoring conditions since a previous temporary protection order was issued on July 28, and then rescinded on Aug. 8, as farmers and ranchers dealt with increased wildfire risk in the region.

The salmon are endangered and the ministry says more than 200 chinook have entered the watershed at a critical stage in their life cycle.

The order now in effect means 458 surface water and groundwater licences and transitioning groundwater users in the watershed must stop using water for irrigation of forage crops, lawns, fairways and garden industrial purposes.

The ministry says those impacted will be contacted directly with a copy of the signed order.

It says provincial staff will continue monitoring streamflow, fish populations and watershed conditions throughout the season, and the order will be rescinded as soon as possible.

It says that will come “once conditions improve sufficiently to protect fish populations and critical environmental flows.”

“If a wildfire or firefighting occurs in the area of the temporary protection order, the Water Sustainability Act allows for water to be used,” the release says.

It notes that programs are in place to support farmers who experience crop failure due to drought, noting B.C.’s Agriculture Ministry is available to answer their questions and respond to claims.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 19, 2026.

items.body:
Canada-U.S. Minister Dominic LeBlanc smiled widely beside U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade czar in Washington on Wednesday as they touted a draft deal which appears to have averted a new round of punishing tariffs on Canada.

United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he feels confident the agreement will protect American workers and jobs while strengthening the North American market, making the continent a manufacturing and energy powerhouse.

“We certainly, I think, have eliminated some of the irritants that we’ve had over the past year,” he said, “We also are taking a strong foot forward.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement that the new deal reinforces and builds on Canada’s existing trade advantages with the U.S. 

LeBlanc and Greer had their latest meeting the morning after Trump announced a three-day pause on 50 per cent tariffs that were set to slam an array of Canadian goods just after midnight Wednesday.

LeBlanc did not provide many details about the specifics of the draft agreement he had hammered out with Greer during weeks of heightened negotiations. He did say Canada’s dairy supply managed system would remain intact.

Multiple news reports have said the deal will see the United States lower sectoral tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal both reported the duties would be reduced from the current 50 per cent levels to 25 per cent.

A source with knowledge of some terms of the agreement but who is authorized to speak publicly about them told The Canadian Press that lower duties on steel and aluminum were part of the deal but could not say how the tariff rate would change.

LeBlanc returned to Ottawa Wednesday to meet with Carney and hold other meetings to put finishing touches on Canada’s side of the trade negotiations. 

Greer said he will brief Congress and American stakeholders on what the two sides have been talking about.

A source with knowledge of some terms of the agreement but who is authorized to speak publicly about them told The Canadian Press that lower duties on steel and aluminum were part of the deal but could not say how the tariff rate would change.

LeBlanc returned to Ottawa Wednesday to meet with Carney and hold other meetings to put finishing touches on Canada’s side of the trade negotiations. 

Greer said he will brief Congress and American stakeholders on what the two sides have been talking about. 

Members of the prime minister’s advisory council on Canada-U.S. relations, who were briefed about the deal Tuesday night, welcomed the tariff pause but said uncertainty continues to harm Canadian businesses.

Lana Payne, Unifor national president, said the “devil is going to be in the details” of the agreement. 

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party was relieved to hear there was a deal in the works but repeated his claim that any agreement must include zero tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber as well as an exemption to the “Buy America” policies.

The deal could come together by Trump’s latest deadline, said William Pellerin, a partner in international trade at McMillan LLP in Ottawa. 

Unlike CUSMA negotiations, Pellerin said this would amount to adjustments to tariffs on the margins — those rates and retaliatory measures can be adjusted with letters, executive orders in the U.S. or an order-in-council on the Canadian side.

But Pellerin also cautioned that there’s very little Canada can do at this stage to hold the United States to its word. He noted Trump has gone back on tariff deals struck with other countries.

“We have to understand that any deal that we strike could get overturned and that we’re buying temporary relief,” Pellerin said.

items.title: Some GTA homes sold in under two weeks last month
items.description: New Wahi data shows where GTA homes are moving fast and where sellers are waiting longest
items.content: <p>New Wahi data shows where GTA homes are moving fast and where sellers are waiting longest</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639227650280910057.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: New Wahi data shows where GTA homes are moving fast and where sellers are waiting longest
items.body:
Homes in one Etobicoke neighbourhood sold in an average of just 10 days in July, while properties in a midtown Toronto enclave spent nearly two-and-a-half months waiting for buyers. That's a striking divergence that underscores how unevenly conditions remain across the Greater Toronto Area (GTA).

New analysis by Wahi, which examined GTA neighbourhoods with five or more transactions last month, found Alderwood in southwest Etobicoke was the region's fastest-selling market in July.

On the other hand, Chaplin Estates in Old Toronto led the slowest tier, with homes averaging 77 days on the market before selling.

The spread between the two poles narrowed from June, when the fastest GTA neighbourhood recorded a six-day average and the slowest reached 126 days.

Housing type also plays a role. According to the Wahi report, condominiums and detached homes tend to attract different segments of the buyer pool, which can influence how quickly properties move.

Established communities dominated by single-family homes, like Alderwood, tend to clear faster than wealthier enclaves where luxury detached properties draw a narrower group of purchasers.

Where homes are moving quickly

The communities leading July's fastest-selling rankings share a common profile: established, family-oriented neighbourhoods with strong transit access, good schools, and a concentration of single-family homes priced to attract a broad buyer pool.

Alderwood's quiet residential streets and relative affordability within the 416 made it accessible to a wider range of purchasers than many inner-city alternatives.

Palmer in Burlington ranked second at 15 days, its tree-lined streets, schools, and central community park making it a natural draw for families.

Uptown Ajax, tied third at 16 days with Dovercourt Park in Old Toronto, benefited from its proximity to Highway 401 and convenient retail access — factors that matter to buyers weighing commute times.

Dovercourt Park's walkability, Bloor Street access, and transit connections similarly reduced its days on market.

Six neighbourhoods tied at 17 days to round out the top ten: Humber Bay in Etobicoke, Timberlea in Milton, Bullock in Markham, Ashburn in Whitby, Victoria Park Village in North York, and Seaton Village in Old Toronto.

Markets where sellers are facing a longer wait

The five slowest-selling GTA neighbourhoods in July ranged from 62 to 77 days on market.

After Chaplin Estates, the list included Tansley Woods in Burlington at 71 days, Bronte Lakeshore in Oakville at 65 days, and Burlington Waterfront at 64 days.

The Queen Street Corridor in Brampton rounded out the group at 62 days, a figure only marginally higher than the 61-day average it recorded in June 2026, per the Wahi analysis.

Wider market conditions continue to shape buyer behaviour across the region.

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board (TRREB), in its 2026 Market Outlook and Year in Review report, forecast GTA average home prices between $1 million and $1.03 million for the year.

An Ipsos consumer poll conducted for TRREB found GTA homebuying intentions declined five percentage points to 22% in 2026 compared to 2025, with 45% of intending buyers identified as first-time purchasers.

items._ogDesc: Canada’s mortgage growth is slowing down, but households are racking up consumer credit as distress borrowing accelerates.
items.body:
The great Canadian borrowing binge continues, but it’s not for mortgages. At least, not entirely. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household debt grew in June, but not as fast as usual. Mortgage credit is weighing down growth as it decelerates post-low rate boom. It’s consumer credit that’s booming, a trend the industry attributes to a rise in “distress borrowing.”

Canadian Household Debt Is Slowing, But Not Slow

Canadian household debt: Annual growth rate.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Household debt grew 0.6% (+$21.0 billion) to $3.29 trillion in June, up 4.3% (+$136.4 billion) from last year. The annual growth rate is the detail worth paying attention to here, as it’s starting to stall and grind lower. That’s not deleveraging, but the pace of borrowing is definitely slowing down.

Canadians Add $100 Billion In Mortgage Debt Despite Slowdown

Canadian household debt: Annual growth rate of mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage debt is the lion’s share of household debt. The segment grew 0.6% (+$13.8 billion) to $2.45 trillion in June, 4.2% (+$98.2 billion) higher than last year. Even as housing markets struggle to gain momentum, households added almost $100 billion.

Households Flock To Consumer Credit As Distress Borrowing Booms

Canadian household debt: Annual growth rate of consumer credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Consumer credit is another story, as its growth now outpaces mortgage debt. The segment added 0.87% (+$7.23 billion) to hit $835.0 billion in June, up 4.8% (+$38.3 billion) from last year. Annual growth is at a pace only seen in 4 months in the past 16 years, even outpacing general household debt growth. This is a much more troubling trend than it sounds.

The acceleration in consumer credit post-mortgage boom often presents liquidity concerns. It’s well documented that after buying a home, borrowers tap credit to supplement depleted finances. The trend is amplified by consumption smoothing or distress borrowing, according to TransUnion. Households are increasingly tapping higher interest revolving credit to absorb rising costs. The recent insolvency boom suggests this plan isn’t working out as well as many had hoped.

items.title: Trump's three-day tariff pause puts Canada deal in focus
items.description: A last-minute pause buys time but leaves Canada's mortgage market in limbo
items.content: <p>A last-minute pause buys time but leaves Canada's mortgage market in limbo</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639227586390240486.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A last-minute pause buys time but leaves Canada's mortgage market in limbo
items.body:
United States President Donald Trump paused threatened 50% tariffs on nearly $28 billion of Canadian goods late Tuesday, citing a breakthrough in negotiations that could determine the conditions for Canada's mortgage market recovery heading into the fall.

Trump announced the three-day reprieve in a social media post less than two hours before the levies were set to take effect at 12:01 AM ET on Wednesday on a wide range of Canadian exports, including wine, dairy, lumber, cement, clothing, and hockey equipment.

The pause expires at the close of business Friday, August 22, setting a tight new deadline for negotiators on both sides of the border.

Prime Minister Mark Carney declined to characterise the development as a done deal.

"Substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done," his office said in a statement Wednesday.

Canada-US Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc returned to Washington early that morning alongside Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, for a second round of talks at the office of US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer.

"We have a bit more work we need to do," LeBlanc told reporters on his way into the meeting.

Trump, speaking separately to reporters, described the outcome as "a very good deal" for both countries, saying he expected Canadian tariffs on American goods to be "totally eviscerated, down to zero."

He also said the US agreed to "readjust" its tariff rates on Canadian autos without specifying by how much.

What's on the table for mortgage markets

The latest tariff threat would have compounded existing levies on steel, aluminium, autos, and lumber — inputs that feed directly into construction costs and, ultimately, the affordability of new housing stock.

Tariff-related uncertainty and its growing impact on Canada's housing market has shadowed mortgage professionals throughout 2025 and into 2026.

Canadian home sales fell 1.9% in 2025 compared with the prior year, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA), with tariff-related economic anxiety pushing buyers to the sidelines throughout much of the year.

A resolution that lifts the cloud of trade uncertainty could be as consequential for buyer confidence as any Bank of Canada rate cut.

The central sticking points in negotiations have included auto tariffs, changes to Canada's dairy quota system, and the reinstatement of American liquor on provincially run store shelves.

A proposal circulating in the final hours of talks would lower tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles from 25% to 15%, with the effective rate potentially falling to approximately 7.5% for vehicles with sufficient US content, still higher than Canada's negotiating position.

Trump also raised the possibility of reviving the long-dormant Keystone XL pipeline, which would carry Alberta oil to US Gulf Coast refineries.

Three days to close — and what comes next

For Canadian mortgage professionals, the next 72 hours could bring either badly needed clarity or another extension of the stop-and-start uncertainty that has suppressed buyer activity since Trump first threatened sweeping tariffs on Canadian imports in January 2025.

Greer posted on social media that the framework agreement in principle covers "comprehensive market access for all American goods, economic security commitments, digital trade alignment, and many important provisions" for both sides, though neither government had released formal documentation as of Wednesday morning.

Businesses on both sides of the border have warned repeatedly that tariff uncertainty, even when the levies themselves have not fully materialised, is already disrupting supply chains and dampening investment.

For Canada's mortgage industry, a clean resolution by Friday would represent the clearest signal yet that the conditions for a sustained housing market recovery are finally beginning to take shape.

items.title: Four straight monthly gains can't hide how far Canada's housing market has to go
items.description: July data shows incremental progress, but national resales remain 12% below the decade-long average
items.content: <p>July data shows incremental progress, but national resales remain 12% below the decade-long average</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639227547873924500.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: July data shows incremental progress, but national resales remain 12% below the decade-long average
items.body:
Canada's housing market extended its winning streak in July. Home resales rose for a fourth consecutive month, edging up 0.5% from June on a seasonally adjusted basis. However, the pace of that improvement makes plain how much ground the market still needs to recover.

According to RBC Economics' July monthly housing market update, national transactions came in at 457,500 annualized units, roughly 12% below the 10-year average.

At the rate of advance recorded over the past two months, it would take more than two and a half years for activity to return to that long-run norm, assistant chief economist Robert Hogue noted in the report.

That arithmetic alone captures the market's predicament. New listings fell a further 1.6% in July from June, reducing earlier concerns that a concentration of mortgage renewals could produce a wave of distressed selling. 

Canadian home sales extended their recovery in July, with the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) reporting a fourth consecutive monthly gain as tightening supply and stabilising prices nudge the national market closer to balance.https://t.co/GDRsSHHZVC — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) August 18, 2026

A floor appears to be forming under home prices

The national aggregate MLS Home Price Index rose for a second consecutive month in July, back-to-back gains not recorded since early 2024, according to Hogue.

That sequential advance, however tentative, signals that the cyclical price floor may be in place at the national level, even if the road to recovery from there is a slow one.

The rebalancing has been driven partly by stabilizing inventory in Ontario and British Columbia, where listings had accumulated rapidly over the past three years.

Ontario is showing the clearest signs of momentum: resales climbed in Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London, and Ottawa in July, with benchmark values rising in Toronto and Ottawa. Year-over-year, however, transactions and prices across most of the province remain below 2025 levels.

Regional fortunes continue to diverge

British Columbia remains in a slump. Province-wide prices declined again in July, led by Vancouver and the Fraser Valley, with a setback in Vancouver offsetting monthly gains in Victoria and the Fraser Valley.

Alberta has stabilized since spring, with prices edging higher across the province, while Edmonton's MLS Home Price Index benchmark returned to positive year-over-year territory in July.

Markets that previously outperformed nationally — among them Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Québec, and Atlantic Canada — are showing signs of topping out. Monthly resale declines hit Regina, Saskatoon, Winnipeg, Montréal, Québec City, Moncton, and Prince Edward Island in July.

Annual price gains in major Québec markets, including Montréal and Québec City, have fallen to less than half the pace recorded at the start of 2026. Halifax's MLS HPI slipped below year-ago levels in both June and July.

CREA's revised 2026 forecast has identified Ontario as the only province expected to record annual sales growth this year, a projection that now has tentative momentum behind it.

Hogue cautioned, however, that any acceleration in national activity will be gradual, held back by static interest rates, slowing population growth, and lingering economic uncertainty.

items.title: Mortgage anxiety rises as Canada's final pandemic-era renewals land
items.description: Royal LePage data shows most Canadian mortgage holders are coping, but anxiety is climbing fast
items.content: <p>Royal LePage data shows most Canadian mortgage holders are coping, but anxiety is climbing fast</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639227528144450951.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Royal LePage data shows most Canadian mortgage holders are coping, but anxiety is climbing fast
items.body:
The final cohort of Canadians who secured pandemic-era mortgages at record-low rates has arrived at renewal. While most households are managing the shift, one in three borrowers is entering the process more anxious than before. That is the central finding of the Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey, conducted by Burson using the Leger Opinion online panel.

The survey of 1,127 Canadian mortgage holders, fielded between July 20 and August 6, found that 38% expect their monthly payment to increase at renewal. That's down from 57% who anticipated a rise in early 2025.

A further 31% expect payments to stay roughly the same, while 17% expect a decrease.

This final group represents approximately 12% of all outstanding mortgages in Canada: five-year, fixed-payment loans originated when the Bank of Canada's overnight lending rate sat at 0.25% in 2021.

Sarah Albert of Premiere Mortgage Centre says refinances, debt consolidation, and proactive planning are helping many borrowers manage higher renewal rates while keeping monthly budgets on track.https://t.co/2Gkw9kTE2e — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) August 7, 2026

One in three borrowers feel more anxious at renewal

Nationally, 35% of respondents say they feel more anxious heading into renewal than they did at their previous one, while 43% report feeling roughly the same.

Anxiety is most concentrated among homeowners who last renewed when rates were at their historic floor.

Among those expecting a higher payment, 76% say it will pressure household finances. Forty-six percent describe that strain as slight, while 30% say it will be significant. Despite this, 71% say they will not change their living arrangements to reduce housing costs.

"The pandemic-triggered era of ultra-low rates came to an abrupt halt in early 2022, having lasted less than two years," said Phil Soper, president and CEO of Royal LePage.

"The final major group of rock-bottom rate holders are up for renewal, and understandably, they are concerned."

Respondents in Saskatchewan and Manitoba are most likely to expect a higher monthly payment at renewal (43%), while Albertans are least likely to do so (29%).

Mortgage renewal wave has hit hardest among newcomers and recent first-time buyers, with 67% of newcomers at payment risk according to a separate Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) survey.

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and expert at LowestRates.ca in Toronto, recently said that "even a modest increase in the rate can change the household budget quickly."

Delinquencies rise slightly, but remain near historic lows

Mortgage delinquency rates remain well below pre-pandemic levels, though Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) data shows the national rate — mortgages 90 days or more past due — rose from 0.21% in the fourth quarter of 2024 to 0.24% in Q4 2025.

Toronto saw one of the largest single-market increases among major cities, climbing from 0.20% to 0.29% over the same period.

CMHC's Spring 2026 Residential Mortgage Industry Report confirmed the renewal wave has peaked, while acknowledging pockets of ongoing stress, particularly in high-cost markets.

"What we are finding in practice is that families are managing the transition," Soper said.

"The widespread default crisis many feared simply hasn't materialised — a testament in large part to Canada's prudent lending standards."

Among borrowers expecting financial pressure at renewal, 58% plan to cut discretionary spending, 48% will reduce travel, and 38% intend to delay home renovations.

A further 8% of respondents have already extended their amortization period. At renewal, 43% of candidates plan to select a fixed rate, while 39% say they will assess all options before deciding. Just under half (49%) intend to stay with their current lender, while 44% plan to compare alternatives.

Homeowners appear far from panic mode on mortgage renewals despite elevated borrowing costs, a picture the Royal LePage findings broadly confirm.

items.title: Asia Standard Americas Proposes Third Condo Tower On Vancouver's Robson Street
items.description:
With their two-tower Landmark On Robson project now complete, Asia Standard Americas — the North American subsidiary of publicly-traded Hong Kong-based developer Asia Standard International Group — now appears ready to add a third tower to the street.

Landmark On Robson — a 34-storey tower and a 32-storey tower with a total of 237 strata units — is located at 1400 Robson Street, making up the entire block between Nicola Street and Broughton Street in the West End of Vancouver.

The third tower is proposed for 1394 Robson Street, a lot located immediately east, on the other side of Broughton Street, that was formerly home to the Robstonstrasse Hotel and is currently being used as a community garden.

Asia Standard Americas acquired the property in 2018 for a reported $24,780,000, and has previously proposed a five-storey commercial building with two levels of office space above three levels of retail space.

The site is currently zoned C-6 and does not need to be rezoned for Asia Standard Americas’ proposal, which is for a 19-storey tower with 72 residential units — 57 strata units and 15 social housing units — above two levels of commercial space.

The 72 units have a suite mix of 14 studios, 26 one-bedrooms, 26 two-bedrooms, and six three-bedrooms. The units have sizes of 369 sq. ft for studio units, 549 or 553 sq. ft for one-bedroom units, 780 sq. ft for two-bedroom units, and 1,551 or 1,578 sq. ft for the three-bedroom units, with the social housing units generally larger than their condo counterparts. The condos will be located above the social housing units.

The building will also include 2,020 sq. ft of indoor amenity space and 4,919 sq. ft of outdoor amenity space. Amenities will be located inside and above the two-level commercial podium.

Renderings of the tower proposed for 1394 Robson Street in Vancouver. (Arcadis, Asia Standard Americas)

With no minimum parking requirements now across the City of Vancouver, the developer is proposing to provide 25 vehicle parking spaces and 158 bicycle parking stalls in a two-level underground parkade. The application notes that the parkade will be accessible from the rear lane, Rosemary Brown Lane, via a car elevator.

The residential entrance will be located along Broughton Street, while the commercial component will be accessible from Robson Street.

“Entrances are designed to establish a desirable and strong identity for the development, contributing positively to Robson Street’s street scape and integrating well into the overall facade design,” the development application states. “All entrances will be clearly distinguishable through their architectural design and treatment.”

Renderings of the tower proposed for 1394 Robson Street in Vancouver. (Arcadis, Asia Standard Americas)

“Situated at the convergence of these two distinct urban conditions, the project occupies a rare transitional site where the warmth of the West End meets the precision of Coal Harbour,” the development application says. “This position informed both the form and the material choice — a pure, uninterrupted rectangular mass responds to Coal Harbour’s clarity and confidence, while brick cladding acknowledges the West End’s textural warmth and neighbourhood belonging.”

“The result is a building that is simultaneously of its place and of its moment,” the application concludes.

Although located directly adjacent to its Landmark On Robson towers, this tower looks architecturally distinct, as those two towers utilize much more glass.

After publishing the development application last week, the City of Vancouver is now accepting public comment on the proposal until Friday, August 28.
